exercise1.prompt: Filtering Rows: Rows at or above the mark

hiddenCases.name: a score exactly on the mark passes
the boundary is included
hiddenCases.describe: a >= comparison, so the mark itself counts

exercise1.hint: At least the mark means the mark passes. A plain greater-than silently fails everyone sitting exactly on the boundary, which is where marks cluster.

exercise2.prompt: Filtering Rows: Pass, fail and unknown

hiddenCases.name: a score of 0 is a fail, not unknown
the counts always total the rows
an empty table is all zeros

exercise2.hint: Test for None first, with "is None", so that 0 is not mistaken for missing. Only then compare with >= mark.

questions.prompt: Why write a filter condition in one place rather than repeating it?
choices: Two copies can disagree after an edit, and both look right
questions.explain: The second copy is the one nobody updates. Two parts of the same analysis then quietly count different people.

questions.prompt: What should you check immediately after filtering?
choices: How many rows you have left
questions.explain: A filter that keeps three rows out of nine hundred is a finding in itself, and usually a mistake in the condition.

questions.prompt: A pass mark of 60 with a > test does what?
questions.explain: Both wordings describe the same off-by-one, and marks bunch at the boundary, so it usually affects more rows than you would guess.

questions.prompt: Why is "if not score" a bad test for a missing score?
choices: A real score of 0 is falsy too, so it would be treated as missing
questions.explain: Use "score is None" when you mean missing. Falsiness lumps 0 in with None.
